newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan premium widens after more DKB arrests.
newsitem.headline: Japan premium widens after more DKB arrests.

text.p: The Japan premium -- the extra cost Japanese banks pay for raising funds in the eurodollar interbank market -- has widened since Friday when another two senior officials of scandal-hit Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) were arrested, traders said on Monday.

With fears of an early U.S. rate rise easing due to a series of weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data late last week, the cost of raising eurodollar funds for major U.S. and European banks has fallen.
But Japanese banks failed to follow suit and were paying higher costs than foreign banks.

This was partly due to doubts about the creditworthiness of Japanese banks in relation to a pay-off scandal involving DKB and Nomura Securities and also because of Japanese banks' steady demand for eurodollar funds covering the end of June, traders said.
The premium for one-month eurodollar deposits was at 7/32 of a point on Monday, against 4/32 a week ago, they said.
Major U.S. and European banks with better credit ratings than Japanese banks are paying 5-5/8 percent in raising one-month eurodollar funds, down from 5-11/16 percent a week earlier, they said.
The premium had stabilised at around 4/32 of a point since jumping to 8/32 on May 20 when prosecutors for the first time raided DKB's headquarters and the homes of several of its officials.
Prosecutors on Friday arrested DKB vice president Ichiro Fujita and another executive on suspicion of making illegal loans to a racketeer.
Friday's arrests brought to 10 the number of DKB officials apprehended in connection with the payoff scandal.
Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who typically extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.
